newsitem.title: USA: Buyback talk lifts Ecuador Bradys, eurobond.
newsitem.headline: Buyback talk lifts Ecuador Bradys, eurobond.

text.p: Ecuador's debt prices got a boost from the expected buyback of $250 million of Brady bonds, traders said.

A local newspaper reported that the Ecuador government would use some of the proceeds from its recent eurobond issues to buy back $200 million face value of par bonds and $50 million of PDI. No government official was immediately available for comment on the report.
Ecuador Pars rose 1/4 to 41-3/4 bid and Ecuador PDI jumped 1/2 to 58.00 bid.

The Ecuador Brady buyback plan had been announced early in the year pending on the eurobond issuance, but the political turmoil in the aftermath of President Abadla Bucaram's outster and the delayed launch of the eurobond casted a great deal of uncertainty on the buyback, analysts said.
Ecuador was seen as taking a calculated risk on the repurchase, they said.
"It reduces the outstanding debt and makes the ratio look better," said Dan Peirce, emerging market debt strategist at Bank of Boston.
With the par bond trading around 42 percent and PDI at 58 percent of the face value, Ecuador would retire the old debt at about half of the cost of the face value , Peirce said.
The buyback of the par bonds, would free $86 million of U.S. Treassury collaterals.
One the flip side, however, Ecuador is replacing the restructured Brady debt of longer maturity with five-year eurobond, which would increase the liability management risk, Peirce said.
Carlos Asilis, analyst at UBS Securities, also considered the buyback "somewhat pre-mature."

Ecuador's ability to service its debt appeared to be sound in the near term, as it has $1.9 billion of international reserve, or enough to cover five months of import, and its debt-to-service ratio is a modest 25 percent, he said.
Thus in the next two years the payment pressure would not increase signficantly, the risk would rise in three to five years, Asilis said.
"Hopefully before then the country would have restructured the debt to extend the maturity," he noted.
Jaime Valdivia, Latin America fixed income analyst at Morgan Stanley, emphasized that the fiscal picture had brightened since Ecuador's Eurobonds were issued on April 18.

Ecuador's fiscal deficit in 1997 is expected to reach 3.6 percent of the gross domestic product (gdp), of which 2.6 percent is already securied from foreign sources and the remaining one percent could be financed internally, he said. The government projected a target of 2.5 percent fiscal deficit to GDP ratio.

The Eurobond, whose launch had been delayed since February, came in two parts. The $150 million seven-year floating rate tranche pays six-month LIBOR plus 475 basis points. The $350 million five-year with 11.25 percent coupon pays 470 bp over U.S. Treasury.
Traders said the five-year fixed tranche was difficult to find on the secondary market.
"With 11-1/4 percent coupon, retail investors don't want to sell," said a trading source.
The floater, which had more in circulation, was bid 102, or about 385 bp over Treasury, he said.
In view of the market demand for the bond and improving economic fundamentals in Ecuador, Valdivia expected the spread to contract to 320 basis points.
Elsewhere in the emerging debts, prices were mixed.
Argentina FRB rose 3/8 to 91-1/4 bid and Brazil C was off 1/4 to 74.00 bid.
